$comment:
The internal media socket between `sitara-realtime` and `sitara-api` (M9-P10b, §25.3). It lands in this package for the reason the package's own rule states: **if both sides of the wire name a set, it belongs here before either side reads it.** The confidence states, the presence states, the memory types and the voice vocabulary all arrived here after the two languages had already disagreed about them; this one arrives before, which is the whole point of having learned it four times.

Why a SECOND socket exists at all. §34.6 is what the BROWSER speaks and it terminates in `sitara-realtime`. Behind it a live call needs two things realtime cannot have: a duplex connection to a speech vendor (no credentials, no provider registry — §3.2 puts those behind `sitara_api.voice.providers`) and the §9 pipeline (no model client, and a second copy of §9 would be a second set of validators to keep in step). A voice NOTE solved the same problem with `POST /v1/chat/ws/voice-note`, because a note is a complete recording and request/response fits it. A call is duplex for its whole length.

Why this is deliberately NOT §34.6. That set is closed at fifteen and is a user-facing protocol. Saying an internal transport in it would mean either widening a closed set under §31.3 change control, or pretending an internal frame was a user-facing event. The two sets are separate and neither borrows from the other.
$binary: 16 kHz mono s16le PCM in BOTH directions — §34.6's format exactly, so nothing in the path transcodes. Upward it is the microphone; downward it is Tara's synthesised reply. Neither is ever written to disk (§13, §33.1: call audio is never stored), and no participant holds a buffer of either beyond the frame in flight. There is no 8-byte header here: §34.6's sequence number exists so a voice NOTE can fail on a gap rather than splice across one, and a live call has no note to fail — a lost packet is a lost moment, not a fabricated sentence.
$typed_directions: The two type sets are DISJOINT, so a frame can never be ambiguous about who sent it. That is worth more than it looks on a socket where one side runs the pipeline on behalf of a user id the other side named.

up_frame.$comment: `sitara-realtime` → `sitara-api`. Realtime owns the §34.6 protocol, the server-side VAD and the session clock; everything it sends here is one of those three speaking.

members.note: a finalised user turn. The API commits the transcript BEFORE running §9 — call audio is never stored, so the transcript is the only record there will ever be, and a provider outage between 'she heard you' and 'she answered' would otherwise erase what somebody said out loud
§25.3's barge-in. Sent by realtime because realtime is where the microphone's PCM is and §25.3 makes the detection server-side
§32.9's metering heartbeat, carrying seconds elapsed. Realtime holds the CLOCK and the API holds the QUOTA, so the arithmetic happens once, on the side that owns the pool
§33.5 evidence realtime observed (§43.5). Realtime has no database
the call is over; meter it into `voice_sessions` (§25.7)

down_frame.$comment: `sitara-api` → `sitara-realtime`. Vendors, validators and the quota all live on this side.

members.note: an STT result. `is_final` is the only branch: an interim becomes §34.6's `captions.partial` (whose role is the constant `user`), a final becomes the turn

a §9 stage NAME and nothing else. No draft, no partial text, no token — the same guarantee `/v1/chat/ws/turn` gives, and the structural reason `captions.partial` can never carry Tara's words even by accident
the whole validated ChatTurn. Always sent BEFORE any audio rendered from it, so a synthesis that dies leaves her words already on screen
synthesis stopped early, with the reason — so realtime can send §34.6's `barge_in` carrying a true reason rather than guessing which of the three it was
§32.9's 5- or 2-minute notice, decided here because the quota is here
§32.9 — the pool hit zero. Never a hard drop: the caller hands off to text

CALL_TICK_INTERVAL_S.$comment: How often realtime reports elapsed seconds for metering. Ten seconds, matching §34.6's heartbeat, so a call carries one periodic obligation rather than two drifting ones. It bounds how late a §32.9 warning can be — never how EARLY the pool can run out, because `exhausted` is evaluated on the same tick.
